claims.statement: Every criterion in cqg resolves to exactly one of three states declared as a closed Literal type — scored, na, or not_evaluated — so the model layer rejects any other status at construction time rather than letting it reach the report.

A criterion may become `scored` only through the `_valid_scored` predicate, which simultaneously requires status scored, an integer score that is explicitly not a bool, a score within the registry scale, and a non-empty justification; any response failing one of these is demoted to not_evaluated.
The judge ignores an `na` status asserted by the LLM and demotes it to not_evaluated, because `na` is a decision owned by the deterministic inventory rather than by the model.

Cross-section aggregation applies the anti-fabrication predicate twice — once to filter contributing sections and once to re-validate the aggregated result as a deliberate safety net — and returns not_evaluated with an explicit French justification when no section produced a compliant score.

When the screening stage routes a document to the light path, score_document makes no LLM call at all and emits every qualitative criterion as not_evaluated rather than inferring a score, a behaviour pinned by a test that verifies zero calls even though the mock provider was configured to return a valid score.

Each non-judged criterion state carries a distinct justification string recording how the value was obtained — "Signal deterministe." for deterministic scores, "Objet absent du document (inventaire)." for inventory exclusions, "Referentiel de questions/cas d'usage absent." for criteria depending on an unshipped external reference grid, and "Route light (crible) : jugement LLM non execute." for the light route.

The golden Q&A workflow keeps a generated answer only when the model explicitly marked it covered with `oui` and the answer text is non-empty; every other case collapses to the marker "Non couvert par le document" with couvert forced to "non", and this fallback is applied independently on both the per-document and the retrieval-grounded corpus-wide paths.
Every golden Q&A row is emitted with statut_validation set to "a_valider", making the generated set a proposal awaiting human validation rather than established truth.

VLM-generated image descriptions injected into the evaluated markdown are wrapped in a tag naming them unverified, and the run counts those occurrences and attaches the count to the document as an `auto_descriptions:<n>` flag so a reviewer can see how much evaluated text was machine-written.

A document whose parsing yields no usable text short-circuits to a DocScore of 0.0 flagged `unreadable`, deliberately skipping metric computation and LLM judgment so no call is spent on empty content.
Only documents with non-empty markdown are appended to the list handed to corpus redundancy detection, which keeps unreadable documents from registering as a cluster of identical documents.

Each document is processed inside its own try/except so that any failure is converted into a persisted DocScore flagged `processing_error: <ExceptionType>` and recorded in the run result, meaning one failing document never aborts the corpus run.

The report surfaces a fixed flag vocabulary as the contract with the human reviewer — `unsupported_format:<ext>`, `unreadable`, `processing_error: <ExceptionType>`, `screen:light (<reasons>)` and `auto_descriptions:<n>` attached by the run orchestration, the four boundary flags `manually_edited`, `missing_sidecar`, `missing_markdown` and `invalid_sidecar` raised while reading a parsed_input/ entry and appended to whichever exit the document took, plus `low_coverage` and `low_parse_confidence` attached during document scoring — joined with `|` into the report's flags column.

not_evaluated criteria are counted rather than hidden: they form the denominator of the coverage figure, so declining to guess mechanically lowers coverage and raises the low_coverage flag instead of being averaged away.

No shipped extension reaches the unsupported_format exit any more: every extension triage admits (.pdf, .txt, .md, .docx, .pptx) has a parser, and the branch is retained deliberately as the landing for a format admitted into SUPPORTED_EXTS ahead of its parser, covered by a test that drives it through triage directly.

The run's error tally counts only the exception path, so neither an unsupported format nor an unreadable document registers as an error — a run reporting zero errors can still contain documents that were never scored, which is why the flags carry the reason.

A corrupt or password-protected office file lands as `unreadable` rather than `unsupported_format`, because parse_document catches the extraction failure and returns an empty document instead of propagating.

The `auto_descriptions:<n>` count is derived from the scored markdown itself, by counting occurrences of the named `AUTO_DESC_MARK` constant with `count_auto_descriptions`, rather than being returned by the enrichment step — so the flag is identical whether the enrichment ran in `cqg parse` or inside `cqg run`.

Reading a parsed_input/ entry yields a document plus a list of flags naming the four ways the human-editable folder can be degraded: `manually_edited` when the markdown's sha256 no longer matches the sidecar's `markdown_hash`, `missing_sidecar` for a markdown dropped in by hand, `missing_markdown` for an orphan sidecar surfaced as an empty document, and `invalid_sidecar` for a sidecar that is no longer valid JSON. None of the four raises; each degrades a single document.

When a hand edit is detected, `blocks_from_markdown` re-derives only the text blocks from the edited markdown and keeps every non-text block — tables and images — together with the image geometry from the sidecar, because those are facts about the source: docling table blocks come from pdfplumber geometry and never appear as pipe tables in the markdown, so re-deriving them from prose is impossible and inventing them is the mistake `_direct_extraction` refuses to make for docx/pptx images.

A parsed markdown is decoded with `errors="replace"` so that a file re-saved in another encoding becomes U+FFFD, which `cid_failure_fraction` already counts and which penalises parse confidence, instead of raising — the same precedent `_plain_text_extraction` set by reading .txt/.md sources as utf-8-sig with `errors="replace"`.

An unsupported_format document is not dropped at the parsing boundary: `parse` writes it into parsed_input/ as an entry with an empty markdown whose category is recorded in the sidecar provenance, and the parsed-entry reader hands that category back, so `run` raises the same `unsupported_format:<type>` flag on either path.

`parse_corpus` isolates each document in its own try/except and collects a failure into the result's `errors` list rather than aborting the corpus; the document is then absent from parsed_input/, and because `parse_document` never raises, what lands on this path is I/O-level failure rather than extraction failure.
